title: Sales HT reads as actual revenue but is Supplier Order planned sell
finding: The company KPI labelled Sales HT aggregates Supplier Order package selling values, while actual Client revenue is represented by confirmed Client Invoices elsewhere.
evidence: CompanyFinancialSummary links Sales HT to /orders. reporting/reports.ts builds it from calculateProjectFinancialSummary(orderInput), whereas Project actual sell uses billing Invoice HT in calculateProjectFinancialPerformance.
whyItMatters: A manager can interpret a procurement plan as invoiced revenue and make an incorrect profitability judgment.
recommendation: Rename the KPI to Supplier Order planned Sell HT and keep Client invoiced HT explicitly separate.

title: Two gross-profit concepts share nearly the same name
finding: Project target-vs-actual gross profit uses Client invoiced HT minus economic cost, while Supplier Order planned gross profit uses Order planned sell minus economic Order cost.
evidence: FinancialPerformanceTable renders performance.actual.grossProfitHt; Supplier Order commercial plan renders report.financial.grossProfit. They are legitimately distinct, not mathematically interchangeable.
whyItMatters: The same Project page can show different gross-profit amounts without an immediate visual explanation of forecast versus invoiced actual.
recommendation: Standardize labels as Actual invoiced gross profit HT and Supplier Order planned gross profit HT, with planning/actual section badges.

title: Landed cost and economic landed cost often show the same value
finding: Landed cost HT excludes VAT; economic landed cost additionally includes non-deductible input VAT. They are usually identical only when all input VAT is deductible or absent, so the concepts are distinct but visually repetitive.
evidence: The production-like runtime sample displayed equal values. The financial calculator adds nonRecoverableInputVat only to economicLandedCost.
whyItMatters: Two identical-looking rows invite users to assume a bug or to ignore the important non-deductible VAT distinction.
recommendation: Keep Economic Landed Cost prominent and collapse pre-VAT Landed Cost under an advanced cost breakdown with a concise distinction.

title: Purchase, landed, and economic cost labels lack a stable hierarchy
finding: Views alternate among Purchase, Purchase cost HT, Landed, Landed cost HT, Economic cost, and Supplier Order economic landed cost.
evidence: Order table, Order detail, Project financial breakdown, portfolio table, and dashboard KPI use different variants.
whyItMatters: Users must infer whether VAT and procurement extras are included from context rather than the label.
recommendation: Adopt Purchase Cost HT, Landed Cost HT, and Economic Landed Cost HT as the three canonical labels.

title: Dashboard repeats the Reports project summary nearly verbatim
finding: CompanyFinancialSummary and ProjectPortfolioTable are rendered unchanged on both the Dashboard and the default Reports view.
evidence: Both routes import and render the same two components; runtime screenshots show the same KPI grid and wide portfolio table.
whyItMatters: Dashboard and Reports have unclear roles, duplicate maintenance surface, and give users little reason to navigate between them.
recommendation: Make Dashboard a compact action-oriented exception view and keep the full portfolio analysis in Reports.

title: Client outstanding and overdue are repeated in adjacent sections
finding: The company KPI grid includes Client outstanding TTC and Client overdue TTC, then the Client Billing card repeats both values immediately below.
evidence: Both render report.clientBilling.outstandingTtc and report.clientBilling.overdueTtc.
whyItMatters: Exact duplication consumes prime dashboard space without adding context.
recommendation: Keep each value once; use the Client Billing section for the full invoiced/received/outstanding story.

title: Twelve equal-weight KPIs obscure operational priority
finding: Project count, planned profitability, cash exposure, overdue amounts, and funding coverage all receive the same card treatment.
evidence: CompanyFinancialSummary defines twelve cards in one uniform grid; runtime inspection showed no primary exception or action hierarchy.
whyItMatters: Users cannot quickly distinguish urgent cash or funding exceptions from contextual totals.
recommendation: Simplify to a small exception-first KPI set and move analytical totals to Reports.

title: Reserved Documents navigation is visible but unavailable
finding: The desktop sidebar contains a Reserved group with a disabled Documents destination.
evidence: navigation.tsx declares /documents with isAvailable false; runtime desktop inspection shows the disabled entry.
whyItMatters: A permanent-looking dead end adds noise and implies missing functionality.
recommendation: Remove the reserved entry until a document feature is explicitly scheduled.

title: Brand subtitle truncates in the fixed sidebar
finding: The Procurement Finance ERP subtitle is visually clipped at the configured desktop width.
evidence: Runtime screenshots show Procurement Finance E… in the sidebar header.
whyItMatters: The primary product identity appears unfinished on every page.
recommendation: Use a shorter subtitle or allocate enough width without expanding the overall navigation.

title: Role and status capitalization is inconsistent
finding: The account role is lowercase, Project status is title case in some views, and Order/payment/report statuses are raw uppercase enum labels.
evidence: Runtime shows admin, Active, ACTIVE, ORDERED, and Operational; many components call replaceAll without case normalization.
whyItMatters: Inconsistent casing makes the interface feel assembled from unrelated modules and weakens scanability.
sourceB: Status rendering across order-table.tsx, portfolio-report.tsx, payments
recommendation: Centralize human status labels in title or sentence case and render them through one badge component.

title: Human-readable dates do not follow one DD/MM/YYYY standard
finding: Payment and Order business dates use DD/MM/YYYY, while Project list and employee metadata use forms such as 01 Jun 2027 or 03 Sept 2026.
evidence: formatDateOnly is centralized for business dates, but project-management.tsx and user-management.tsx contain local date formatting.
whyItMatters: Mixed date formats slow comparison and contradict the stated global display convention.
recommendation: Use DD/MM/YYYY for all day-level values and a separately named formatter only for true timestamp metadata.

title: Financial values wrap into fragmented multi-line cells
finding: Narrow columns wrap amount, decimals, and currency onto separate lines in the desktop Order table.
evidence: Runtime inspection showed values such as 45 / 933.15 / EUR on separate lines; the table contains many financial columns.
whyItMatters: Fragmented figures are difficult to compare and increase the chance of reading the wrong magnitude or currency.
recommendation: Keep financial figures non-wrapping, reduce general-view columns, and reserve the full financial set for the Financial view.

title: General Order view overlaps heavily with the Financial view
finding: The General tab already exposes purchase, freight, other cost, landed cost, selling revenue, and margin-oriented information despite a dedicated Financial tab.
evidence: order-table.tsx defines view-specific column groups; runtime General view remains financially dense.
whyItMatters: The view switch does not create a clear operational-versus-financial distinction and contributes to horizontal scanning.
recommendation: Keep identity, supplier, status, and key dates in General; move detailed cost/revenue metrics to Financial.

title: Supplier Payment view is singular while the domain is plural
finding: The Order list view label uses Supplier Payment, while navigation and operational terminology use Supplier Payments.
evidence: Order view selector and payment section labels use different number.
whyItMatters: Minor wording drift weakens the canonical vocabulary.
recommendation: Use Supplier Payments for the list view and Supplier Payment only for one transaction.

title: Pagination claims page-only selection on tables without selection
finding: The shared footer always says Selection applies to this page only, including Billing and other lists with no visible row checkboxes or bulk action.
evidence: Pagination hardcodes the sentence unconditionally; runtime /billing shows the message without selection controls.
whyItMatters: The footer describes a capability the page does not offer and suggests hidden selection state.
recommendation: Make the selection note an explicit option used only by bulk-selectable tables.

title: Dense filter grids clip labels and hide filter meaning
finding: Several filter selects truncate their selected text, including reporting currencies, billing type, and sort direction.
evidence: Runtime screenshots show All reporting currenci…, Quotes and Invoi…, and Desce…; list forms use fixed multi-column grids without visible labels.
whyItMatters: Users cannot reliably confirm active filters, especially when several adjacent unlabeled controls are present.
recommendation: Use visible compact labels, sensible minimum widths, and a consistent filter toolbar with overflow rows.

title: Clients and Suppliers diverge from the Projects reference table
finding: Directory pages share similar filters but use separate management components and interaction conventions; Projects presents clearer row selection/edit affordances and richer status context.
evidence: ClientManagement, SupplierManagement, and ProjectManagement independently implement table/edit behavior rather than a common Directory pattern.
whyItMatters: Employees must relearn comparable master-data lists and future fixes must be repeated.
recommendation: Standardize Directory table structure and edit affordances on Projects while preserving entity-specific fields.

title: Import Client PDF understates accepted document formats
finding: The action label says PDF although the intake accepts PDF, JPG, and PNG documents.
evidence: Runtime /billing action text and client-document intake file validation differ.
whyItMatters: Users with image scans may assume the supported workflow is unavailable.
recommendation: Rename the action to Import Client Document and mention accepted formats in helper text.

title: Three intake workflows use parallel but independently built review patterns
finding: Supplier quote, Client document, and Item budget intake each implement upload, proposal, validation, and confirmation with different component structures and feedback conventions.
evidence: quote-intake.tsx, client-document-intake.tsx, and budget-import.tsx are separate large client modules with overlapping stages.
whyItMatters: The same review mental model feels different by module and defect fixes can diverge.
recommendation: Standardize shared stage vocabulary, warning layout, and confirmation controls without merging domain-specific schemas.

title: Legacy Order-based Client Receipt direction remains exposed
finding: The Payments page still offers both SUPPLIER_PAYMENT and CLIENT_RECEIPT Order-installment directions even though Client Billing schedules and ClientReceipt transactions are now authoritative for Client cash.
evidence: payments/page.tsx labels Client receipts — cash in and queries PaymentInstallment by direction; Billing separately owns ClientPaymentInstallment and ClientReceipt.
whyItMatters: Employees can see two operational paths for Client cash and may mistake a legacy plan for an authoritative Billing receipt.
recommendation: Make the operational page Supplier Payments only; retain legacy Client Order schedules as read-only historical compatibility where needed.

title: Legacy Client Order schedule calculations coexist with authoritative Billing cash
finding: ProjectReportingSnapshot still calculates a client direction from Order receivable bases and Order PaymentInstallments, while portfolio cash position and Billing summaries use ClientReceipt records.
evidence: projectSnapshot creates client = calculateDirectionPaymentSummary from financial.orders; portfolio Project rows later replace client outstanding and cash position with billing summaries/receipts. The detail table explicitly labels Legacy Supplier Order plan remaining.
whyItMatters: Two client outstanding/cash models coexist in one reporting pipeline, increasing maintenance and interpretation risk even where labels acknowledge legacy status.
recommendation: Deprecate legacy client direction from primary reporting and isolate historical compatibility behind an explicit read-only section.

title: Selling revenue, package selling price, Sell HT, and planned sales overlap
finding: The Order commercial amount appears under several labels, some excluding and some including separately recharged freight.
evidence: packageSellingPrice excludes separately recharged freight; totalSellingRevenue includes it once. UI labels do not always expose that distinction.
whyItMatters: A user cannot know from Selling or Sales alone whether freight resale is included.
recommendation: Use Package Sell HT and Total Supplier Order Sell HT (including separately recharged freight) consistently.

title: Freight planning and recovery are correct but terminology is easy to conflate
finding: Expected Freight Allowance is a Project planning value based on expected purchase cost, while Freight Recovery Target is based on actual freight cost and applicable markup. Both sit in one card with similar monetary emphasis.
evidence: reconcileProjectFreight uses separate projectExpectedProductPurchaseCostHt and actual order/expense inputs; the UI correctly groups Planning and Actual but uses Headroom/Variance as one combined label.
whyItMatters: Employees may expect Order AUTO freight allocations or Client recovery to equal the Project planning allowance.
recommendation: Keep the separate formulas; standardize Freight Headroom as allowance minus recovery target and add a one-line basis tooltip.

title: Freight Variance / Headroom combines two interpretation labels
finding: One value is labelled with both variance and headroom even though its sign is defined as expected allowance minus recovery target.
evidence: reconcileProjectFreight calculates headroomHt; the Project UI labels it Freight Variance / Headroom.
whyItMatters: Variance can conventionally be actual minus plan, the opposite sign, so the combined label is ambiguous.
recommendation: Use Freight Headroom HT and explain that positive means planned allowance exceeds recovery target.

title: Order output VAT and Invoice output VAT need explicit authority labels
finding: Supplier Order reporting retains planned Order output VAT, while Project VAT Position correctly uses confirmed Invoice output VAT. Both are valid but can appear under the generic label Output VAT.
evidence: reports.ts aggregates order.costs.outputVat; Project VAT position receives Billing summary outputVat.
whyItMatters: Planned commercial VAT can be mistaken for the current VAT position payable to the State.
recommendation: Label Order output VAT as planned and reserve Output VAT in VAT Position for confirmed Client Invoices.

title: Payments page title conflicts with the Supplier Payments navigation intent
finding: The navigation and Project links position this area as Supplier Payments, but the page title is Payments and exposes legacy Client receipt direction.
evidence: Navigation says Supplier Payments; page metadata/H1 says Payments; the filter says Both directions.
whyItMatters: The route appears to own all cash transactions although authoritative Client Receipts live under Client Billing.
recommendation: Rename and scope the page to Supplier Payments once the legacy Client direction decision is approved.

title: Project detail presents six tables and multiple dense financial cards at once
finding: The page combines target performance, funding, freight, Order plan, VAT, cash, payment summaries, Order breakdown, cash flow, overdue items, buildings, rooms, and freight expenses.
evidence: Runtime counted six tables on the Project detail route and source renders the full ProjectFinancialDashboard plus management sections.
whyItMatters: Important Project actions and exceptions are buried in a long analytical page.
recommendation: Keep a concise Project overview and collapse detailed commercial, VAT, freight, and cash sections under clear subviews or disclosures.

title: Detail pages use different edit and related-record conventions
finding: Project and Billing details use explicit view/edit shells; Order detail has a large specialized shell; Client and Supplier details emphasize related summaries and return links with different action placement.
evidence: Runtime inspection and separate project-detail, order-detail-shell, billing-detail, and master-data page implementations.
whyItMatters: The expected View → Edit → Save/Cancel pattern changes between entities.
recommendation: Standardize header, back link, status, Edit placement, Save/Cancel footer, and related-record section order.

title: Order editor is a single unusually large interaction surface
finding: The Order form exceeds 1,800 lines and combines identity, dates, buildings, currencies, cost lines, pricing modes, VAT, freight, schedules, live summaries, and historical compatibility behavior.
evidence: src/components/procurement/order-form.tsx is 1,867 lines; runtime Order detail exposed thirteen forms.
whyItMatters: The user must navigate a high cognitive load and small changes carry broad regression risk.
recommendation: Preserve one save transaction but divide the editor into clear commercial, cost/VAT, logistics, and payment sections with progressive disclosure.

title: Draft preservation is shared unevenly across editing models
finding: Several client editors use usePersistentActionState, while native server forms and specialized inline cells use different reset/error behavior.
evidence: use-persistent-action-state.ts is used in large editors, but list inline editors and server-action forms hold drafts independently.
whyItMatters: A validation error or rerender may preserve input in one module but feel different in another.
recommendation: Define one draft/error contract and test it across all authoritative edit paths before consolidating implementations.

title: Inline editing is implemented through several parallel shells
finding: Generic InlineEdit and DetailEditShell coexist with bespoke Project, Order, Billing, Item, Client, Supplier, Room, Location, Payment, and employee editors.
evidence: Client component inventory shows many independent editing modules despite shared Phase 10.3 interaction goals.
whyItMatters: Authorization, draft preservation, dirty-state behavior, and audit messages can drift across entities.
recommendation: Consolidate only the edit state contract and primitives; keep domain forms separate.

title: Portfolio reporting loads broad Order/payment data then filters in memory
finding: The portfolio query gets filtered Projects, but listOrders and listPaymentInstallments are only partly scoped and results are filtered again by Project IDs in application memory.
evidence: getPortfolioReportingSnapshot creates projectIds, then scopedOrders/scopedInstallments with Array.filter after broad service calls.
whyItMatters: Portfolio pages can become slower and more memory-intensive as unrelated historical data grows.
recommendation: Push the resolved Project scope into database filters and measure before changing query composition.

title: Funding coverage adds a heavyweight second-stage list calculation
finding: After fetching the paginated Project list, the page separately loads funding coverage through Order and Billing services for the visible projects.
evidence: projects/page.tsx awaits getProjectsFundingCoverage after its first Promise.all; funding-coverage.ts uses full Order summaries and Billing summaries.
whyItMatters: The reference Directory list may degrade as financial child data grows and delays the full response without a streaming boundary.
recommendation: Create a purpose-built aggregate query or stream the financial enhancement after the core Project list.

title: Many select filters rely on their first option as the only label
finding: Filter controls usually have no visible label and often no aria-label; once a value is selected, its dimension must be inferred from position.
evidence: Projects, Clients, Suppliers, Payments, Orders, Billing, and Reports render adjacent select elements without associated label elements.
whyItMatters: Screen-reader context is weak and dense desktop filter bars become harder to understand after selections change.
recommendation: Add compact visible labels or accessible names to every filter while retaining the dense layout.

title: Date display has local formatters alongside the canonical helper
finding: formatDateOnly provides DD/MM/YYYY, but employee and project components define local date presentation.
evidence: Search finds formatDate in user-management.tsx and locale formatting in project/calendar components alongside domain/payments/dates.ts.
whyItMatters: The technical duplication directly causes visible date inconsistency.
recommendation: Consolidate day-level display formatting and keep explicit month/timestamp helpers only where semantically intended.

title: Enum-to-label formatting is scattered through the UI
finding: Many components expose enum values by replaceAll('_', ' ') with inconsistent lowercasing or no casing conversion; others maintain local label maps.
evidence: Search finds repeated replacements across Orders, Payments, Items, Reports, Calendar, Activity, Supplier detail, and intake components.
whyItMatters: Business vocabulary and capitalization drift whenever a new enum or status is added.
sourceA: Repeated replaceAll calls across src/app and src/components
recommendation: Centralize domain-aware display labels rather than applying one generic enum formatter to every concept.

title: Tables share pagination but not a coherent table contract
finding: Each module builds its own markup for selection, row links, inline editing, empty states, numeric alignment, and overflow behavior.
evidence: OrderTable, BillingTable, ItemTable, PaymentInstallmentTable, three Directory management components, and report tables are independent implementations.
whyItMatters: Visible behavior diverges and cross-cutting accessibility or density fixes require repeated edits.
recommendation: Define shared table behavior primitives and conventions, without forcing every domain into one giant generic table.

title: Billing service and client editor concentrate many responsibilities
finding: billing.ts exceeds 2,000 lines and BillingDetail coordinates document fields, status, schedules, receipts, allocations, reconciliation, and destructive actions.
evidence: File-size inspection: src/lib/billing/billing.ts 2,017 lines; billing-detail and companion editors split UI but share a broad service surface.
whyItMatters: Changes to one billing workflow risk side effects in another and make single-source-of-truth review harder.
recommendation: Split the service by document, schedule, receipt, allocation, and reporting responsibilities behind stable transaction boundaries.

title: Validation feedback has no common page-level contract
finding: Inline cells, full forms, schedule editors, and AI review screens surface errors through different combinations of field text, summaries, banners, and action-state messages.
evidence: Code review across usePersistentActionState, InlineEdit, order-form, billing editors, quote intake, and item import.
whyItMatters: Users cannot predict where to look after a failed save, and accessibility announcements may differ.
recommendation: Define a shared validation-feedback pattern: field issue, summary, preserved draft, focus target, and server error.

title: Report filters change shape by tab without persistent context cues
finding: Project/client/supplier/status filters persist between views, while horizon, direction, and date fields appear or disappear; the page has no active-filter summary.
evidence: viewHref preserves only four shared filters; cashFlowHref and ReportingFilters conditionally build different query controls.
whyItMatters: Users can believe a date or direction filter still applies after switching report views when it has been dropped.
recommendation: Show active filter chips and explicitly reset or preserve view-specific filters when switching tabs.

title: Client billing summaries are represented by overlapping DTOs
finding: ProjectFinancialDashboard defines a local Phase11BillingSummary while Billing services and portfolio reporting expose related but independently shaped summary types.
evidence: Phase11BillingSummary duplicates invoiced, paid, outstanding, overdue, VAT, schedule completeness, and next-due fields from billing summary outputs.
whyItMatters: One business summary can diverge in naming or completeness semantics between Project, Dashboard, and Billing views.
recommendation: Expose one server-owned serialized Client Billing summary contract and derive view-specific subsets from it.

title: Page-level loading boundaries cover whole data-heavy routes
finding: Data-heavy Project and reporting pages await broad query sets before rendering their core content; granular streaming is limited.
evidence: Next App Router route loading files exist, but Project detail and list await complete reporting/funding structures before returning the main tree.
whyItMatters: A slow financial aggregate delays navigation feedback for content that could render independently.
sourceB: Project/report server pages and Next.js streaming guidance
recommendation: After measuring production latency, stream secondary financial panels behind targeted Suspense boundaries.

title: Bespoke interaction surfaces need one keyboard and focus audit
finding: Owned AlertDialog primitives are labelled, but numerous bespoke inline editors, table row interactions, disclosures, and file-review controls have not been verified end-to-end with keyboard focus.
evidence: Source review shows semantic buttons in many places but different composition patterns; runtime sweep did not safely trigger destructive dialogs or every validation state.
whyItMatters: A control can be technically present yet difficult to complete without a pointer or after a server error.
recommendation: Run a focused keyboard/focus pass during the approved cleanup batch and standardize focus return and error focus.

title: Large client boundaries bundle broad workflows
finding: Order, quote intake, Client document intake, and Item table/editor modules are large client components that import most of each interaction flow.
evidence: order-form.tsx, client-document-intake.tsx, quote-intake.tsx, and item-table.tsx are among the largest handwritten TSX files and begin at client boundaries.
whyItMatters: Initial interactivity can require more JavaScript than necessary and component responsibilities become harder to isolate.
sourceA: Client component inventory and file sizes
recommendation: Defer until bundle measurements exist; then narrow client boundaries around truly interactive subsections.
